Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- The European Union will launch its first naval operation Tuesday, protecting vessels from pirate attacks off the coast of Somalia, EU policy chief Javier Solana announced Monday. A French army helicopter taking off from French frigate Nivose,  on patrol in the Gulf of Aden. EU foreign ministers approved the mission during their regular meeting in Brussels on Monday. Solana said the operation is "very important" because EU vessels will be operating "in a place in the world that everybody's looking at because of the new problems related to piracy." "It's very important that we have taken that decision to launch it tomorrow," he added. The EU naval force will take over the role of escorting United Nations World Food Program vessels carrying food and relief supplies to war-torn Somalia, an EU news release said. Its mandate, which is spelled out in several U.N. Security Council resolutions, also will include "the protection of vulnerable vessels cruising off the Somali coast, and the deterrence, prevention and repression of acts of piracy and armed robbery off the Somali coast," the news release stated. The deployment follows a decision by the European Council in September that established a coordination cell that supported surveillance and protection operations by several member states off the Somali coast. Piracy has become increasingly common in that area this year, particularly in the Gulf of Aden. So far, pirates have attacked almost 100 vessels off Somalia's coast and successfully hijacked nearly 40, according to the International Maritime Bureau. Those hijacked vessels include an enormous oil tanker, a chemical tanker, and a ship laden with Soviet-era arms, including tanks. The pirates normally hold the ships for ransom. The Somali-based pirates have extended their reach beyond Somalia's coastline. On Saturday, a Dutch-operated container ship outran pirates off the coast of Tanzania, an IMB official told CNN. A luxury cruise ship carrying more than 1,000 passengers and crew successfully outran pirates off the coast of Yemen last weekend. A multinational fleet -- including vessels from the United States, NATO member states, Russia and India -- has been patrolling the Indian Ocean waters near the Gulf of Aden, which connects the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. Around 20,000 oil tankers, freighters and merchant vessels pass along the crucial shipping route each year. In a recent interview provided to CNN, a pirate leader claimed attacks on shipping would continue so long as life in Somalia remained desperate. "The pirates are living between life and death," said the pirate leader, identified by only one name, Boyah. "Who can stop them? Americans and British all put together cannot do anything."

(CNN) — European Union foreign policy chief Javier Solana said Monday that the EU would begin its first-ever naval mission on Tuesday, with the goal of defending ships against pirate attacks near Somalia’s coast.

The announcement came as a French military helicopter was shown lifting off from the French frigate Nivose, which was patrolling in the Gulf of Aden. EU foreign ministers gave their approval to the operation at their scheduled meeting in Brussels on Monday.

Solana described the mission as “very important,” noting that EU ships would be working in an area that has drawn global attention because of growing piracy-related problems. He added that it was highly significant that the EU had decided to start the operation the following day.

According to an EU statement, the naval force will assume responsibility for escorting United Nations World Food Program ships transporting food and humanitarian aid to Somalia, a country devastated by conflict. The mission’s authority, outlined in several U.N. Security Council resolutions, will also cover the protection of at-risk ships traveling off Somalia’s coast, as well as efforts to deter, prevent and suppress piracy and armed robbery in those waters, the EU release said.

The deployment comes after a September decision by the European Council to create a coordination unit to assist monitoring and protection efforts carried out by several EU member countries off Somalia.

Pirate activity in the region has risen sharply this year, especially in the Gulf of Aden. The International Maritime Bureau says pirates have attacked nearly 100 ships off Somalia and have managed to seize close to 40 of them. Among the captured vessels are a giant oil tanker, a chemical tanker and a ship carrying Soviet-era weapons, including tanks. Typically, the pirates demand ransom in exchange for releasing the vessels.

Pirates operating from Somalia have also begun striking farther from Somalia’s own shoreline. On Saturday, an International Maritime Bureau official told CNN that a Dutch-operated container ship escaped pirates by outrunning them off Tanzania. The previous weekend, a luxury cruise ship with more than 1,000 passengers and crew members aboard also managed to speed away from pirates near Yemen.

A multinational naval presence, including ships from the United States, NATO countries, Russia and India, has been monitoring Indian Ocean waters close to the Gulf of Aden, the channel linking the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea. About 20,000 oil tankers, cargo ships and other commercial vessels use that vital route every year.

In a recent interview made available to CNN, a pirate leader said attacks on ships would not stop as long as conditions in Somalia remained desperate. “The pirates are living between life and death,” said the leader, identified only as Boyah. “Who can stop them? Americans and British all put together cannot do anything.”

The mission, known as **Operation Atalanta**, will escort vulnerable ships, including vessels carrying humanitarian aid for the World Food Programme, and patrol waters off the coast of Somalia, where pirate attacks have surged in recent months.

EU officials said the operation marks a significant step for the bloc’s common security and defense policy, bringing together warships, surveillance aircraft and maritime coordination teams from several member states.

Pirate groups operating from Somalia’s largely ungoverned coastline have increasingly targeted ships in the region, hijacking vessels and demanding multimillion-dollar ransoms.

The EU mission is expected to work alongside naval forces from NATO, the United States and other countries already operating in the area. Commanders say the goal is to deter attacks, respond to distress calls and ensure the safe delivery of food aid to Somalia, where millions depend on international assistance.

Somalia has not had an effective central government for years, creating conditions that have allowed piracy to flourish. International shipping groups have urged governments to increase naval patrols, warning that continued attacks could disrupt global trade and drive up shipping costs.

**EU Foreign Ministers Approve Naval Mission to Combat Piracy off Somalia**

**Brussels** — European Union foreign ministers have approved a naval operation off the coast of Somalia aimed at protecting humanitarian aid shipments and deterring a surge in piracy that has threatened one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.

The mission, expected to involve warships and surveillance aircraft from several EU member states, will focus on escorting vessels carrying food aid for Somalia under the United Nations World Food Program, as well as protecting vulnerable commercial shipping in the Gulf of Aden and the waters off the Horn of Africa.

EU foreign policy chief **Javier Solana** welcomed the decision, saying the operation reflected Europe’s determination to respond collectively to the worsening security crisis at sea. Solana said the mission would help ensure that desperately needed humanitarian supplies reach Somalia, where years of conflict and drought have left millions dependent on international assistance.

He also stressed that piracy had become not only a regional problem but an international threat, disrupting trade and endangering seafarers. The EU, he indicated, had a responsibility to contribute to efforts already under way by NATO, the United States, Russia, India and other naval powers operating in the area.

The naval mission is designed in part to provide regular escorts for **World Food Program** shipments. WFP vessels have repeatedly required military protection to deliver food to Somali ports, especially Mogadishu. Without escorts, aid agencies have warned that ships may refuse to sail into Somali waters because of the risk of hijacking. The World Food Program has said that maritime protection is essential to feeding hundreds of thousands of Somalis.

The EU decision comes amid a sharp rise in piracy incidents off Somalia. Pirate gangs operating from Somalia’s largely lawless coastline have seized dozens of vessels, often holding ships and crews for ransom. In recent weeks, attacks have drawn global attention because of the size and value of the ships targeted.

Among the most dramatic incidents was the hijacking of the **Saudi-owned supertanker Sirius Star**, carrying a large cargo of crude oil. The ship was seized far out in the Indian Ocean, demonstrating the pirates’ expanding range. The capture shocked the shipping industry and underscored the growing sophistication of Somali pirate groups.

Pirates have also continued to hold the **Ukrainian-operated cargo ship Faina**, which was carrying tanks, weapons and ammunition when it was seized. That case raised particular concern because of the military nature of the cargo and the potential risk that arms could fall into the hands of armed groups in the region.

Other commercial vessels, including container ships, bulk carriers and fishing boats, have been attacked or hijacked in the Gulf of Aden, a key route linking Europe and Asia through the Suez Canal. Shipping companies have increasingly called for stronger naval protection, while some have considered rerouting vessels around the Cape of Good Hope, a longer and more expensive journey.

The EU mission represents one of the bloc’s most significant maritime security operations. Its mandate is expected to include deterring and disrupting pirate attacks, escorting humanitarian shipments, and coordinating with other international naval forces in the area. Officials have emphasized that the operation will work under international legal authority, including United Nations Security Council resolutions allowing action against piracy off Somalia.

Somalia has lacked an effective central government for years, creating conditions in which pirate networks have flourished. Armed groups have taken advantage of weak coastal security, poverty, and the absence of law enforcement to build a lucrative ransom industry. International officials say combating piracy at sea is necessary, but they also acknowledge that a lasting solution depends on restoring stability and governance inside Somalia.

The EU’s approval of the mission signals growing concern that piracy off Somalia is no longer an isolated criminal issue but a major challenge to humanitarian relief, regional security and global commerce.

**BREAKING NEWS**  
**December 8, 2008 | Brussels/Nairobi**

### EU Launches Naval Mission to Fight Piracy off Somalia

The European Union has launched a naval operation off the coast of Somalia in a major effort to deter escalating pirate attacks and protect vulnerable ships traveling through the Gulf of Aden, one of the world’s busiest maritime trade routes.

The mission, known as **Operation Atalanta**, marks the EU’s first-ever naval deployment. Warships and maritime patrol aircraft from several European nations are being sent to the region to escort humanitarian aid deliveries and safeguard commercial vessels threatened by armed pirate gangs operating from Somalia’s lawless coastline.

EU officials said the force will focus on protecting ships carrying food aid for the **World Food Programme**, as well as other vulnerable vessels transiting the Gulf of Aden and waters off the Horn of Africa. The route is a critical corridor linking Europe, the Middle East and Asia through the Suez Canal.

Piracy off Somalia has surged sharply in recent months, with attackers using speedboats, automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenades to seize merchant ships and demand large ransoms. The hijackings have raised alarm among shipping companies and governments, prompting some vessels to reroute around southern Africa at far greater cost.

The EU deployment comes amid growing international concern over security in Somali waters, where the collapse of central authority has allowed piracy networks to flourish. NATO and U.S.-led naval forces have also been operating in the area, but officials say the scale of the threat requires broader coordination.

EU commanders said the mission will patrol high-risk areas, escort aid shipments, monitor suspicious vessels and intervene where possible to prevent attacks. The operation is expected to run for an initial period of one year.

Somalia has been without a stable central government since 1991, and its long coastline has become a base for pirate groups targeting tankers, cargo ships and relief vessels. International agencies warn that attacks on aid shipments could worsen the humanitarian crisis in the country, where millions rely on food assistance.

Shipping industry representatives welcomed the EU move but cautioned that naval patrols alone may not end the crisis unless instability on land in Somalia is addressed.

## Somali piracy surge prompts EU naval mission as global powers move warships into Gulf of Aden

**NAIROBI, Kenya** — A sharp rise in piracy off the coast of Somalia has turned one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes into a high-risk corridor, prompting the European Union to launch a new naval operation and drawing an expanding international military response.

The EU mission, known as **Operation Atalanta**, is aimed at protecting commercial vessels and humanitarian aid shipments traveling near Somalia, particularly through the **Gulf of Aden**, a key route linking the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and the Suez Canal.

The operation comes after a series of high-profile hijackings that have highlighted the growing reach and boldness of Somali pirate groups. In recent months, pirates have seized tankers, cargo ships and vessels carrying sensitive goods, often holding crews hostage while demanding multimillion-dollar ransoms.

Among the most dramatic incidents was the hijacking of the **Sirius Star**, a Saudi-owned supertanker carrying crude oil. The vessel was captured far from the Somali coastline, demonstrating that pirate groups were no longer operating only in coastal waters but had expanded deep into the Indian Ocean.

Another major seizure involved the **MV Faina**, a Ukrainian-operated cargo ship carrying tanks, weapons and ammunition. Its capture raised international concern over where the military cargo might end up if pirates or armed groups gained access to it.

Pirates have also targeted smaller cargo vessels, chemical tankers and commercial ships from several nations, disrupting maritime trade and increasing insurance and security costs for shipping companies.

Somalia’s long-running instability has been a central factor in the rise of piracy. The country has lacked a strong central government for years, leaving its coastline — one of the longest in Africa — largely unpoliced. Pirate networks operating from coastal towns have taken advantage of the security vacuum, using speedboats, satellite phones and “mother ships” to track and capture commercial vessels.

The EU’s naval mission is part of a broader international effort to secure the waters near Somalia. The United States, NATO, Russia, India, China and other countries have deployed naval forces to the region or increased patrols. Warships have escorted merchant vessels, responded to distress calls and, in some cases, intervened during pirate attacks.

The United States has also supported multinational maritime task forces operating in the area, while NATO ships have helped escort World Food Programme vessels carrying aid to Somalia. Those shipments are considered critical, as millions of Somalis depend on humanitarian assistance.

Despite the growing military presence, officials say stopping piracy remains difficult. The area to patrol is vast, and pirates often operate from small boats that are hard to detect until they are close to a target. Once a ship is seized and hostages are taken, military options become limited because of the risk to crew members.

Shipping companies have begun adopting additional security measures, including rerouting vessels farther from the Somali coast, increasing speed through dangerous waters, posting extra lookouts and using barbed wire, water cannons or private security teams.

But analysts say a lasting solution will require more than naval patrols. They argue that piracy is tied to conditions on land, including poverty, lawlessness and the absence of effective governance in Somalia.

For now, the surge in hijackings has transformed piracy from a regional security problem into a global maritime crisis — one that has forced governments and navies from around the world to respond.

**EU Takes Over Protection of U.N. Food Aid Ships Bound for Somalia Amid Pirate Threat**

**BRUSSELS/MOGADISHU —** The European Union has taken over responsibility for protecting United Nations food aid shipments to Somalia, launching a naval security mission as pirate attacks intensify in the Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden.

The operation is aimed primarily at safeguarding vessels chartered by the U.N. World Food Programme, whose deliveries are a lifeline for millions of Somalis facing conflict, drought and chronic food shortages. Aid officials say the threat of hijacking has repeatedly disrupted shipments and raised the cost and complexity of getting food into the country.

European warships and surveillance aircraft are expected to escort aid vessels through waters off the Horn of Africa, one of the world’s busiest and most dangerous maritime corridors. The mission also includes patrols intended to deter attacks on commercial shipping.

Somalia’s long coastline has become a hub for piracy in recent years, with armed groups operating from lawless coastal areas and targeting cargo ships, tankers and humanitarian vessels. Pirates have increasingly moved farther into the Indian Ocean, using speedboats and sometimes “mother ships” to stage attacks far from shore.

The EU mission marks one of the bloc’s most prominent naval operations and follows earlier international efforts to protect shipping in the region. NATO and individual countries have previously provided escorts for U.N. aid deliveries, but European officials say a coordinated EU force will offer a more sustained response.

The World Food Programme has warned that without naval escorts, shipowners may refuse to carry aid to Somalia. Most of the food assistance for the country arrives by sea, and any interruption could have severe consequences for displaced families and vulnerable communities.

Piracy off Somalia has also become a major concern for global trade. The Gulf of Aden links the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and Suez Canal, making it a critical route for vessels traveling between Europe and Asia. Shipping companies have reported rising insurance costs and, in some cases, have rerouted ships around southern Africa to avoid attacks.

European officials said the mission is designed to protect humanitarian deliveries while supporting broader international efforts to improve maritime security. However, analysts caution that naval patrols can only address the symptoms of piracy, not the instability on land that allows pirate networks to operate.

Somalia has lacked effective central governance for decades, and poverty, armed conflict and the absence of coastal law enforcement have contributed to the growth of piracy. Many pirate groups have portrayed themselves as defenders of Somali waters, though their operations have evolved into organized criminal enterprises seeking ransom payments.

Aid agencies welcomed the EU deployment but stressed that the humanitarian situation inside Somalia remains precarious. Fighting, displacement and limited access continue to hamper relief work, even when supplies reach port.

For now, U.N. officials say armed escorts are essential to keeping food shipments moving. As pirate attacks continue to threaten vessels across the region, the EU mission is expected to play a central role in ensuring that aid reaches Somalia’s ports safely.
